advisor.summary: For a mixed business-personal trip, the deductible outcome is largely settled before departure. Domestic transportation is all-or-nothing on the trip's primary purpose under Reg. §1.162-2(b): a primarily business trip deducts the full airfare even with personal days attached; a primarily personal trip deducts none of it, however real the work performed. Lodging and meals follow the day count either way, and the counting rules reward planners — travel days count, client-required standby days count, and a weekend sandwiched between business days counts when going home is impractical. Foreign trips face a stricter allocation regime under §274(c), with two safe harbors worth building into the itinerary, and spouse costs are nondeductible absent employee status and a bona fide role. Advisory: the value lies in trip design and a contemporaneous file, not in a number the engine can honestly compute.
mechanics: Under Reg. §1.162-2(b), domestic transportation turns entirely on primary purpose, with time devoted to each activity the most important factor — win the day count and the round-trip fare deducts in full; lose it and the fare is wholly personal.
On-site costs allocate by day whatever the transportation answer: lodging, meals at 50 percent under §274(n), and local costs deduct only for business days.

Business days include travel days, days a client requires presence even if little work occurs, and intervening weekends or holidays when returning home is impractical — meetings on Friday and Monday make the weekend count for lodging and meals.

Foreign travel requires allocating transportation between business and personal days under §274(c) unless the trip runs one week or less or personal time stays under 25 percent — safe harbors to design into the schedule, not discover afterward.

Spouse and companion costs are nondeductible under §274(m)(3) unless the spouse is a bona fide employee traveling for a genuine business purpose — and even then lodging deducts at the single-room rate, not half the double.

§274(d) places travel in the strict-substantiation category — amount, dates, destination, and business purpose, recorded contemporaneously; the practical standard is a per-trip file of itinerary, meeting confirmations, and receipts assembled during the trip.

authority.note: Strict substantiation forecloses estimation — a reconstructed travel file is a losing one.

requirements: A genuine business purpose for the destination, documented before departure.
A day-by-day itinerary separating business from personal days, retained with calendar entries and confirmations.
Transportation and lodging receipts gathered during the trip, not at filing time.
For spouse costs: employee status and a genuine business role, or exclusion of those costs.
risks: The leading audit theory is the vacation with a meeting attached: a trip that is really personal fails the primary-purpose test and zeroes the transportation deduction — and under the Sanford strict-substantiation line, reconstructed records leave no estimate to fall back on.
Foreign trips outside the safe harbors demand an allocation many preparers never make — an automatic adjustment on exam.
Spouse airfare and the double-room premium claimed without employee status are a recurring, easily spotted adjustment.
Aggressive day counts invite recharacterization of the entire trip — an hour of email does not make a business day.
stateNotes: Conformity: travel deductions sit inside federal business income, so conforming states absorb them with no separate computation.
PTET interaction: entity-paid travel reduces the pass-through entity tax base like any other ordinary deduction; the strategy needs no separate PTET step.
Missouri: conforms through its federal starting points (RSMo §143.121, §143.431) and makes no travel-specific modification.
reviewChecklist: Trip files exist and were assembled contemporaneously — itinerary, confirmations, receipts.
Primary-purpose determination supportable from the day count on every mixed trip.
Foreign trips tested against the one-week and under-25-percent safe harbors.
Spouse travel tied to employment status and a documented role, or excluded.

client.teaser: A few smart scheduling habits turn more of every trip into a deduction.
client.headline: Plan your trips so the business part really gets deducted
plainEnglish: When a trip mixes work and fun, the tax result depends on how you build the trip. Here is the surprising rule for U.S. trips: if the trip is mainly business, the whole airfare is deductible — even with beach days attached. If it is mainly personal, none of the airfare counts.

Hotels and meals follow the days. Business days count; personal days do not. The calendar is a tool here: meetings on Friday and Monday can make the weekend between them count too. And keeping an overseas trip inside certain time limits protects the whole fare.

The other half is one simple habit. Keep a small trip file — itinerary, meeting confirmations, receipts — as you go. It takes minutes, and it separates deductions that survive questions from deductions that vanish.
client.analogy: Two travelers can take the same trip and spend the same money — yet only the one who planned the calendar gets the deduction.
